title: The Myrrhbearer at the Tomb
subtitle: Selected passages from the Gospels
source: Text drawn from the King James Version (1611, public domain). Editorial framing by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: Out of whom went seven devils
sections.framing: Mary of the village of Magdala first appears in Luke's Gospel in a short list of women who travelled with the Lord and the Twelve through Galilee, providing for them out of their own means. Luke mentions her by name and notes, almost in passing, what had brought her into that company. The seven demons are not described and the manner of her deliverance is not told; the Gospel records only that she had been freed, and that her gratitude took the form of a life of service.
paragraphs: And it came to pass afterward, that he went throughout every city and village, preaching and shewing the glad tidings of the kingdom of God: and the twelve were with him,
And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils,
And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance.
notes: The Orthodox Church has never identified Mary Magdalene with the unnamed sinful woman of Luke 7 or with Mary of Bethany; that conflation is a Western tradition arising in the sixth century. In the East she is honored as a virtuous disciple from her first appearance in the Gospel.

The number seven, in the biblical idiom, denotes completeness rather than a literal count. The Fathers read her deliverance as a total liberation, and her later steadfastness as the answer of a soul that had been brought wholly back.

sections.title: Standing by the Cross
sections.framing: The Gospel of John names by name the women who did not leave the Lord at his death. The disciples had fled; Mary the Mother and the disciple whom Jesus loved had been given to each other from the Cross; and at a small distance, watching, stood the women who had served him from the days in Galilee. Of these John names three, and Mary Magdalene is one. She had been given much, and she did not turn away when the cost was demanded.
paragraphs: Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.
notes: She is named also among the women at the burial (Matthew 27:61, Mark 15:47), watching where the body was laid. The Fathers note that her constancy at the tomb on the morning that followed is the natural fruit of this constancy at the Cross.

sections.title: The first witness of the Resurrection
sections.framing: Of all the Gospels' Resurrection accounts, John's is the most personal. He tells the encounter as if Mary herself had told it to him. She comes to the tomb while it is still dark, finds the stone rolled away, and runs to fetch Peter and the beloved disciple. They look in, see, and go home. She remains, weeping. And when she turns, the Risen Lord himself is standing in the garden, and she does not know him until he speaks her name. The whole Church has read the scene ever since as the pattern of every soul that finally hears itself called.
paragraphs: But Mary stood without at the sepulchre weeping: and as she wept, she stooped down, and looked into the sepulchre,
And seeth two angels in white sitting, the one at the head, and the other at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.
And they say unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? She saith unto them, Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him.
And when she had thus said, she turned herself back, and saw Jesus standing, and knew not that it was Jesus.

Jesus saith unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou? She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away.
Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.
Jesus saith unto her, Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father: but go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God.
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken these things unto her.
notes: Because she was the first to see the Risen Lord and was sent by him to the apostles with the news, the Orthodox Church calls her Equal-to-the-Apostles, and the Fathers gave her the title 'apostle to the apostles.'

Her feast is kept on the twenty-second of July, and she is commemorated together with the other myrrhbearing women on the third Sunday of Pascha. The tradition relates that she afterwards went to Ephesus and laboured with the Apostle John, and that she reposed there in peace.

sections.title: Christ is risen
sections.framing: A widely-repeated tradition relates that after the Lord's Ascension Mary Magdalene travelled to Rome to bear witness, and was received in audience by the emperor Tiberius. Holding out an egg as a sign of new life, she greeted him with the words that have echoed through every Orthodox Pascha since: Christ is risen. The Church does not place the tradition in the Gospels, but keeps it in her hymnody, and the painted red egg of the Paschal feast is held to be its memorial.
paragraphs: And taking an egg in her hand, she said: Christ is risen.
Greater than the apostles in her love, and first of all who saw the Risen Lord, she did not cease to proclaim his Resurrection until her own falling asleep.
notes: The Tiberius story is found in late Byzantine sources and in Russian iconography, where Mary is often shown holding a red egg. The Orthodox Church receives it as a pious tradition rather than Gospel, and uses it to teach the missionary character of the Resurrection.
